title: Haptic/Graphic Rehabilitation: Integrating a Robot into a Virtual Environment Library and Applying it to Stroke Therapy
protocol: Sensory feedback affects learning and adaptation.
Explore whether artificially increasing sensory feedback promotes faster learning or adaptation.
Apply greater sensory feedback forces or visual cues to enhance mistakes.
Provide adequate neurological stimulus to promote higher levels of adaptation or learning through error augmentation.
Deviate outcomes of motor control actions from the ideal.
Self-adjust internal model according to the magnitude of error.
Approach external environment as internal model adjusts, decreasing task execution errors.
Prolong practice of functionally relevant activities for restoration of function.
Investigate if new technology applications can enhance current therapeutic practices beyond dosage increases.
Combine specialized robotic devices with computer displays to augment feedback of error.
Use human-machine interaction studies to speed up or trigger motor relearning.
Create a wrapper for HAPI in the haptics library by creating your own .cpp and header file.
Place HAPIWAM.cpp into the source directory: HAPI/src
Place HAPIWAM.h into the header file directory: HAPI/include/HAPI
Include the main header file(s) of your robot at the top of HAPIWAM.h, in this case for the Barrett WAM: extern "C" { #include <include/btwam.h> }
Include <HAPI/HAPIHapticsDevice.h> in HAPIWAM.h.

Create your class and include the following 4 functions in HAPIWAM.h: bool initHapticsDevice(int); bool releaseHapticsDevice(); void updateDeviceValues(DeviceValues &dv, HAPITime dt); void sendOutput(HAPIHapticsDevice::DeviceOutput &d, HAPITime t).
Ensure your class inherits publicly from the HAPIhapticsdevice class.
Create a header guard for your class in HAPIWAM.h.
Define static DeviceOutput and static HapticsDeviceRegistration attributes under the HAPIWAM class.
Define static member functions for callbacks in HAPIWAM.cpp.
Define your constructor and destructor in HAPIWAM.cpp.
Register your device in HAPIWAM.cpp.
Go to HAPI/HAPI/build and edit CMakeLists.txt.
Add dependent libraries after the line that says 'SET(OptionalLibs)' in HAPI/HAPI/build/CMakeLists.txt.
Navigate to HAPI/HAPI/build through a command console.
Type cmake .
Type sudo make.
Type sudo make install.
Edit CMakeLists.txt in H3DAPI/build directory.
Rebuild H3DAPI library by typing cmake . in H3DAPI/build directory.
Type sudo make in H3DAPI/build directory.
Type sudo make install in H3DAPI/build directory.
Create a finite state machine for the targeted reaching program.
Allocate a target at the start of the trial.
Set target locations randomly or from a file for each trial.
End the start of the trial once user launches toward the target above velocity threshold, typically 0.06 meters per second.
Begin the launch state after the start of the trial ends.
Transfer to Target Contact state upon touching the target or staying inside it for a specific period.
Enable the Target Contact state during the Launch state when the target is touched.
End the Target Contact state once the subject stays within the target for a specific period.
Transition to the End of Trial state after the Target Contact state ends.
Signal the data collection software to mark the end of each trial in the parsing method used by the developer.
Enable the Start of Trial state unless it is the final trial.
Upon qualifying for the study, evaluate each participant's functional ability.
Conduct the evaluation by a blind rater at the start and finish of each treatment paradigm.
Include a one-week follow-up after each evaluation and an overall 45-day follow-up.
Perform a range of motion (ROM) assessment in the VRROOM.
Conduct clinical measures including Box and Blocks Assessment, Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT).
Assess Arm Motor Section of the Fugl-Meyer (AMFM) and Assessment of Simple Functional Reach (ASFR).
Utilize an exotendon glove with wrist splint to assist in neutral wrist and hand alignment.
Attach the center of the robot handle posterior to the radiocarpal joint on the forearm.
Use a spring-powered Wilmington Robotic Exoskeleton (WREX) gravity-balanced orthosis to lessen the patient's arm weight.
Instruct the patient to chase a cursor presented in front of them, moved via a tracking device by the therapist.
Patients practice three days per week for approximately 40-60 minutes.
Work together in a trio with the therapist and robot.
Sit side-by-side with the therapist.
Connect the patient's wrist to the robot.
Begin each session with five minutes of passive range of motion exercises (PROM) with the therapist.
Spend ten minutes situating the patient in the machine.
Complete six blocks of movement training lasting five minutes each.
Rest for two minutes between each block of movement training.
View two cursors on the stereo display during training.
Manipulate one cursor while the participant controls the other.
Instruct participants to follow the exact path of the therapist’s cursor.
Establish an instantaneous error vector e as the difference in position between the therapist’s and participant’s cursors when deviation occurs.
Magnify visual error by a factor of 1.5e (m) during training.
Apply an error augmenting force of 100e (N/m), which saturates at a maximum of 4 N for safety reasons.
